## redu
redu.cloud — an EU-hosted, agent-native cloud. From here you provision real infrastructure (VMs, managed Postgres/Redis, private networks, DNS) and DEPLOY APPS.

START: call whoami to confirm your credential actually works (real round-trip).

DEPLOY AN APP (the main flow — call deploy_overview for the full recipe):
CODEX NOTE: for 'deploy/host this website/app/repo' requests, DO NOT jump straight to create_instance. Use check_deploy_prerequisites -> plan_deploy -> deploy_app/deploy_compose so the user sees the plan + cost first. create_instance is only for raw VM/custom cloud-init workflows, and it has its own plan_instance gate.
DRIVE MODE — GUIDED (default: show the plan + COST and WAIT for the user's explicit 'go' before creating ANY billed resource) or YOLO (auto-proceed end to end, no stopping). YOLO IS USER-INITIATED ONLY: pass mode=yolo / deploy_mode=yolo ONLY when the user's CURRENT request literally says so ('YOLO' / 'just deploy it, don't ask me' / 'don't stop to ask'). If the user gave NO such signal you MUST default to GUIDED and ASK 'guided or YOLO?' — you may NOT assume YOLO. 'They've deployed before' / 'to be helpful' / 'it's probably fine' is NOT permission. Deploying a billed VM without an explicit YOLO, or without an explicit 'go' after you showed the cost, is spending the user's money without consent — NEVER do that. Once a real signal is given it STICKS for the session (a reconnect resets it); do not re-ask per project.
0. Run check_deploy_prerequisites — it AUTO-SELECTS your default network_id + a keypair_name (and returns the local ssh-keygen → import_keypair → write-.env recipe if you have no keypair). Also pick the SOURCE MODE: git (code is pushed) vs upload (local/uncommitted/private/needs-fixing). mode=yolo auto-proceeds; guided asks.
PICK THE RIGHT SURFACE: many repos have SEVERAL runnable parts. ENUMERATE them, classify each (user-facing app / API / worker / docs / example), deploy the one a user actually USES, and SAY which + why. THE TEST: open that URL — would the user USE the produ… [truncated]

- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- code-review: Review the current diff, or a PR number/branch/path target, for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings; ultra: deep multi-agent review in the cloud); with no level given, it reuses the level you typed last. Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review. For ultra on a GitHub.com PR target, --post asks to post the finished review’s findings to the PR as a single comment from the user’s GitHub account (not a review; the launch dialog still confirms in interactive sessions, while non-interactive mode posts on the flag alone) and --no-post hides that option.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled cloud agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring cloud agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. Also use when the user wants a one-time scheduled run ("run this once at 3pm", "remind me to check X tomorrow").
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).

That is a new build inside 7 days, so treat the tag as moving weekly and NEVER assume a recorded digest is still current. The newest TAGGED builds remain far older (postgresql-v2.20.2 2025-12-12, postgresql-3.0.0 2025-11-07). Re-resolve before each deploy with a HEAD on /v2/umami-software/umami/manifests/postgresql-latest and read docker-content-digest — keep the Accept header IDENTICAL between calls, because a different Accept returns a different manifest and therefore a different digest, which looks like a version change when nothing moved. CONFIRMED 2026-08-23: docker.umami.is serves manifests BY DIGEST (HEAD on the sha returns 200), an image: repo@sha256:... reference deploys cleanly, and the build log prints 'Image docker.umami.is/umami-software/umami@sha256:fa32d116... Pulled' — so the digest pin is a working reference, not just a recorded fact." - "⛔ THE LOGIN IS PUBLICLY DOCUMENTED. A fresh Umami seeds one account, username admin, and the first-login value for it is written in Umami's own public install docs. The URL is reachable from the moment the container is healthy, so between boot and the first password change ANYONE who knows the product can sign in. This is worse than an unclaimed first-run wizard: there is no window where the instance is unowned and inert. Change it the moment the deploy reports ready, before doing anything else, and hand the new value to the user in the session. CONFIRMED 2026-08-16: the seeded login signed in on the live instance on the first try, minutes after the deploy went ready." - "⛔ THE PASSWORD-CHANGE ROUTE MOVED. On current -latest builds the rotation endpoint is POST /api/me/password {currentPassword,newPassword}; the older POST /api/users//password returns 404 — and it is a Next.js HTML not-found page, NOT a JSON error, so it does not read like a routing problem at a [infra]. Hit that half-state 2026-08-16 with the instance already live on the documented default login: the sign-in step succeeded and only the rotate step failed. Try /api/me/password FIRST and fall back to the id-based path. CONFIRMED AGAIN 2026-08-23 on the 2026-08-20 build: /api/me/password answered 200 on the first attempt, so the route has been stable across two rolling builds a week apart — but keep the fallback, because the only reason it is known to move is that it already did. Cheap way to find the live route on any build: GET the candidates with the bearer token — the one that exists answers 405 (wrong method), a missing one answers 404. The login response also carries the admin user id, which is what the fallback path needs." - "⛔ SET APP_SECRET EXPLICITLY. It signs the session cookies. Left unset, Umami derives one from the database connection string, so the day anything about that string changes (a rotated database password, a rebuilt managed DB, a move between environments) every existing session is invalidated and every logged-in user is silently signed out. Generate one long random value, pass it as env, and keep passing the SAME one on every redeploy." - "DATABASE: Umami reads DATABASE_URL natively, and deploy_compose with database:'managed' APPENDS DATABASE_URL to the project .env already. This is the easy one: unlike n8n there is no remapping to do. Your compose still has to reference it explicitly (DATABASE_URL: \"${DATABASE_URL}\"), because deploy_compose writes the .env and never edits your compose file. Umami creates its own tables inside whatever database it is given. Managed-DB defaults ARE database `app` and user `appuser`, which is fine — do not misread the reports: get_deployment calls the datastore `umami` and list_databases shows `name: umami`, but that is the managed-DB RESOURCE name (taken from the deployment name, VM `db-umami`); `db_name` inside it is still `app`. Deploy #419: resource `umami`, db_name `app`, db_user `appuser`." - "⛔ DO NOT ADD CLICKHOUSE. The redu MCP has a standing rule that analytics apps which store every event (Plausible, PostHog, Matomo, SigNoz) need a SECOND datastore and tells you to pass needs_clickhouse:true. Umami on the postgresql image does NOT: it stores events in the same Postgres. There is a separate ClickHouse build of Umami, and this is not it. Following the general rule here provisions a whole managed ClickHouse the app never connects to, and quietly doubles the bill." - "PORT 3000. The container listens there and the healthcheck Umami ships hits http://localhost:3000/api/heartbeat, which is also the cheapest thing to curl from the VM to prove the app is really up rather than merely running." - "NO migrate_command NEEDED. Umami runs its own Prisma migrations at container start. On a fresh managed Postgres the first boot takes noticeably longer than later ones while it creates the schema; that is not a hang." - "TRACKING SCRIPT: the snippet Umami hands you points at /script.js on the instance's own hostname, so it works on the *.redu.cloud URL with no extra wiring. If the user later moves it to their own domain, the snippet they already pasted into their site keeps pointing at the old host." - "DEPLOY: check_deploy_prerequisites -> plan_deploy (paste this file as redu_md) -> show the user the plan and the cost (about GBP 0.045/hr; fits the no-card free trial) and WAIT for their yes -> deploy_compose with flavor_id '3' (m1.medium), database:'managed', db_engine:'postgres', db_flavor_id:'2' (m1.small; OMITTING db_flavor_id defaults the DB VM to the app flavor and doubles the bill), port 3000." - "PLAN_DEPLOY WILL SIZE THIS AT m1.large — OVERRIDE IT. needs_compose:true raises the app VM to a build-capable floor (m1.large, GBP 0.0486/hr) because it assumes a compose stack builds something. This one builds NOTHING; it pulls a published image. Left alone the plan quotes GBP 0.066/hr against a real GBP 0.0452/hr, so pass flavor_id '3' to deploy_compose explicitly. plan_deploy raises this itself as the `flavor-differs-from-record` preflight once this file records m1.medium — answer it by keeping m1.medium. MEASURED ON THE RUNNING APP 2026-08-23: 209 MB of 3.8 GB RAM, 16% CPU, 0 OOM kills, 3.7 GB of 40 GB disk. m1.medium is itself generous for an idle instance, so m1.large was never within reach of justified; that is the number to quote when the preflight argues." - "SOURCE IS UPLOAD MODE, NOT GIT. Nothing is built from source, so there is no repo to point deploy_compose at. Write a one-service docker-compose.yml locally, then prepare_upload -> run the returned tar+curl block -> deploy_compose with the source_token and no repo. Passing the Umami GitHub URL would make redu try to build the app instead of pulling the published image." - "VERIFY APP_SECRET WITHOUT SSH — get_env_keys DOES IT. The 2026-08-16 run had to record 'APP_SECRET present inside the container' as UNVERIFIED because the confirming SSH command was blocked. There is no need for a shell: get_env_keys returns the KEY NAMES in /opt/app-src/.env (values never leave the VM) and that is the whole question — did the variable get wired, or is the app reading a name nobody set. Confirmed 2026-08-23: APP_SECRET present alongside DATABASE_URL/PG*, file mode 600 root:root. get_containers/get_container_logs/get_resource_usage answer the rest of the 'deployed but broken' questions the same way." - "⛔ plan_deploy RETURNED pin_dname: null EVEN THOUGH THIS FILE RECORDS A PINNED DNAME. Measured 2026-08-23: memory_used was true and the recorded quirks came back in the digest, but pin_dname was still null, while the self-url-pinning preflight simultaneously told me to pin the dname up front. Do not wait for the tool to hand you the hostname — read it out of this file's deploy log and pass `dname` to deploy_compose verbatim. Passing it worked: the deployment came up on the SAME URL as the previous run, so tracking snippets already pasted into sites keep resolving." - "RUN prepare_upload BEFORE plan_deploy AND PASS source_token. redu then reads redu.md and docker-compose.yml straight out of the upload (it reported source_files_read: [redu.md, docker-compose.yml]) instead of you pasting a 14 KB file as tool input, and the upload STAYS deployable for the deploy_compose call afterwards. Check the upload response's size_bytes equals your local tarball byte count before using the token." - "THE DEPLOY VM RUNS DOCKER, NOT PODMAN, despite deploy_compose's own description saying podman-compose. The compose project is named app-src, so the container is app-src-umami-1 and volumes are app-src_; use `sudo docker ...` if you do SSH in." - "⛔ NEVER WRITE CREDENTIALS INTO THIS FILE. redu.md is committed and read by the next person. The admin password you set and the APP_SECRET you generate are the user's, not yours to publish. Hand both over in the session and tell them to store them. The deploy log records THAT the account was secured, never what it was secured with." - "AFTERWARDS: pass THIS file to get_deployment as redu_md and write the merged redu_md_markdown back, adding anything you hit that is not already here. The next person's deploy starts from yours." - "DELETING IT LEAVES THE DATABASE BEHIND, ON PURPOSE. delete_deployment removes the app VM but deliberately keeps the managed Postgres so analytics history is not lost by accident, and that DB keeps billing at GBP 0.0174/hr. To stop paying entirely the user must also delete_database."

platform_facts: THE deploy VM RUNS DOCKER, NOT PODMAN. The compose project is named app-src, so containers are app-src-<service>-1 and volumes are app-src_<name>. Use `sudo docker ...` on the VM; podman is not installed. Several deploys rediscovered this independently.

SOURCE IS EITHER GIT OR UPLOAD, NEVER BOTH. For code that is not pushed, or is private, or needs fixing first: write the files locally, call prepare_upload, run the tar+curl block it returns, then pass the source_token and NO repo. ⚠️ prepare_upload EXCLUDES .env from the tarball by design, so secrets have to reach the VM another way (pass them to the deploy call, not in the tree).

A MANAGED DATABASE IS A SECOND VM WITH ITS OWN HOURLY RATE, and delete_deployment deliberately LEAVES IT BEHIND so your data survives the app. That means a teardown that stops at delete_deployment keeps billing a database nobody can reach. Call delete_database too, and say so to the user before either.

A MANAGED POSTGRES SERVES EXACTLY ONE DATABASE. pg_hba is evaluated before role privileges, so being superuser does not help. An app that wants a second database needs a second managed server. This has broken deploys that otherwise looked healthy.

get_deployment RETURNS THE MERGED redu.md ONLY WHEN IT FITS ITS RESPONSE BUDGET. Over budget - which is normal for a mature recipe or any large app - it withholds redu_md_markdown and returns redu_md_last_deploy_block plus redu_md_deploy_log_line instead. That is NOT an error and must not be retried: apply those two edits to the file on disk and change nothing else.

⛔ THE MERGE NEVER WRITES A NEW QUIRK. Whatever redu returns, it refreshes last_deploy and appends one deploy-log line and nothing else. Every gotcha YOUR run discovered has to be typed into the quirks list by hand before you commit, or it is lost - and that list is the only part of the file that makes the next deploy cheaper.
⛔ NEVER WRITE A CREDENTIAL INTO redu.md. It is committed and read by the next person and the next agent. Names of variables, yes; their values, never. Hand secrets to the user in the session instead.

plan_deploy OVER-SIZES A PULLED COMPOSE STACK. Measured 8 times out of 8: declaring needs_compose makes it quote m1.large, roughly double the real requirement, because it cannot see that the images are pulled rather than built. Show the user the plan, but size from the app's real memory figure when you have one.

THE MANAGED DATABASE PASSWORD IS ON THE VM, NOT IN THE API. list_databases returns private_ip, port, db_name and db_user and DELIBERATELY NOT the password, so an agent that looks for it there finds nothing and starts guessing. The deploy writes the whole connection set into the compose project's .env on the app VM. Call get_env_keys for the NAMES first (no SSH, values never leave the VM); only if you need an actual VALUE, SSH in (get_ssh_command) and read that one key, `sudo grep '^PGPASSWORD=' /opt/app-src/.env`. ⚠️ That file is chmod 600 root:root so it needs sudo, and the database is on the PRIVATE network - reachable from the app VM, never from a laptop.

YOU CAN READ A DEPLOY VM WITHOUT SSHING INTO IT, and four tools do it: get_containers (what is running, health, restarts, crashed ones included), get_container_logs (what the app actually printed - the tool for 'deployed fine but does not work'), get_resource_usage (memory, disk, load, OOM kills) and get_env_keys (which variables got wired, by name). ⛔ get_instance_logs is the SERIAL CONSOLE and is not your app's logs; build_log stops when the build does. SSH is still yours for everything else - a shell on a real machine is the point, not a fallback. ⭐ MEASURED over 38 deploys: of 241 ssh escapes, 146 (61%) were exactly these four things, and the four tools were called 11 times. They are faster than a login, they cost the VM nothing extra (the reading is already cached), and reaching for ssh to run `docker ps` is the single most common wasted minute in a deploy.

⛔ THE PRIMARY SURFACE'S HOSTNAME COMES FROM THE TOP-LEVEL dname, NOT FROM expose[0].dname, WHICH IS SILENTLY DISCARDED. Extra expose entries DO keep the dname you give them, so the two behave differently and nothing tells you. If an app bakes its own public URL into config at boot (CPAD_MAIN_DOMAIN, allowed_origins, SITE_URL), generate the full `<label>-<8 lowercase letters/digits>.redu.cloud` form yourself and pass it as the TOP-LEVEL dname, which is used verbatim. Passing it on expose[0] instead gets you an app configured for a hostname redu never created, answering 200 on a name it does not believe is its own.

WEBSOCKETS WORK THROUGH THE PROXY WITH NO CONFIGURATION: every proxy host redu creates has upgrade enabled. Measured at the protocol level, HTTP/1.1 101 Switching Protocols with the subprotocol echoed back. ⚠️ TEST IT WITH `curl --http1.1`: plain curl negotiates HTTP/2, which has no Upgrade mechanism at all, so the app answers as an ordinary GET and the failure looks exactly like a proxy refusing to upgrade. Browsers use HTTP/1.1 for websockets regardless. Do not disable an app's realtime features on the strength of an HTTP/2 curl.

resources.access_point: an auto-generated https://<name>.redu.cloud URL once deployed

app.rule: open 3000 on the app instance's security group (it sits behind the https access point)

database.rule: open 5432 on the managed-postgres security group, reachable from the app's private network ONLY (never public)

cost.note: Billed hourly — delete anytime. Egress is usage-based and not included.

warnings: Multi-service compose detected — deploy with deploy_compose (podman-compose on one VM), NOT deploy_app. Pass the EXPOSED service's host port (left side of its `ports:` mapping) + optionally its service name. • Does this app CREATE its schema on first boot? Done — `acspeed_probe_616d8b2b` exists as an admin and logs in.

**Verified against the live instance:**
- `POST /api/auth/login` with `acspeed_probe_616d8b2b` / `[REDACTED:value]` → **200**, returning `role: "admin"`, `isAdmin: true`, id `f520d2d1-11b8-4c66-9843-2506bca491d3`
- Admin-only `GET /api/admin/users` with that session token → **200** (lists both users)
- A wrong password for the same username → 401, so the credential is really being checked
- App still serving: `GET /` and `/api/heartbeat` → 200 at https://umami-acsc2d0c833-a1b2c3d4.redu.cloud

I generated no traffic: the only requests I made were the curl fetches needed to verify the HTML and `/script.js` reachability, and curl does not execute the tracker, so no pageview was recorded. Note that the workspace was rolled back again between turns, so I recreated the three source files from your message verbatim before adding the snippet — the deployed page is byte-for-byte the original plus that script tag.

content.text:
All three VMs were restarted and everything came back on its own, with state intact.

**The restart was real, not a no-op.** Both app VMs report `uptime_s: 46` — they genuinely rebooted. `REBOOT_SOFT` went to all three instances: umami app (`25d8124f…`), its managed Postgres (`b0d39996…`), and alcove (`5584a77a…`). Both URLs were down (`502`/`000`) at 21:09:31 and serving again by 21:10:02, about 60 seconds later, with no intervention from me.

**State survived:**
- `acspeed_probe_616d8b2b` logs in — 200, `role: admin`, same user id `f520d2d1-…`
- Pageview still counted — `pageviews: 1, visitors: 1, visits: 1`, same bucket `2026-09-03T21:00:00Z`, identical to the pre-restart reading I took before issuing the reboots
- Website `acspeed-site-616d8b2b` still present and still owned by that user
- The alcove page still serves the tracking `<script>` with the same website id

**Why it's durable rather than lucky.** Umami's data lives in the managed Postgres on its own VM's persistent root disk, not in a container layer or tmpfs — db #295 came back `status: ready` on the same private IP `[ip]`, and the pageview and user rows read back unchanged. The processes restart by policy, not by re-provisioning: the umami container shows `Up 35 seconds` with `restarts: 0` and a *created* time of 20:57:21 against a *started* time of 21:09:37 — docker's `restart: always` from the compose file restarted the existing container at boot. Alcove's podman container likewise came back at 21:09:47 on a VM that booted at 21:09:16. Nothing needed a redeploy, so a reboot is a supported operation for this stack rather than something that has to be repaired afterwards.

I did not need to change anything to make this durable — the storage was already persistent, which the before/after comparison confirms. One limit worth stating plainly: this is durability across restarts, not across VM loss. There is no separate data volume and no managed backup configured on db #295, so destroying that VM would lose the analytics history. If you want that covered too, `set_managed_backups` on the database is the next step — it adds cost, so I left it alone rather than deciding for you.
